frontHtml: What is the denominator of an incidence rate?
backHtml: Total person-time at risk (e.g. person-years) contributed by people free of the disease.

frontHtml: Cumulative incidence vs incidence rate: which needs a stated time frame and assumes complete follow-up?
backHtml: Cumulative incidence (risk); it is a proportion over a defined period.

frontHtml: In a steady state, how are prevalence, incidence and duration related?
backHtml: Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration.

frontHtml: A treatment prolongs survival without curing. Effect on incidence and prevalence?
backHtml: Incidence unchanged; prevalence rises.

frontHtml: Case-fatality vs cause-specific mortality: what is each denominator?
backHtml: Case-fatality: people with the disease. Cause-specific mortality: the whole population at risk.

frontHtml: What is the standardised mortality ratio?
backHtml: Observed deaths ÷ expected deaths (expected from reference age-specific rates applied to the study group).

frontHtml: Which standardisation method suits a small occupational cohort with unstable age-specific rates?
backHtml: Indirect standardisation (SMR).

frontHtml: Who is excluded from the denominator of a secondary attack rate?
backHtml: Index cases and contacts who are already immune.

frontHtml: Denominator of the infant, neonatal and postneonatal mortality rates?
backHtml: 1,000 live births.

frontHtml: Age range for neonatal vs postneonatal deaths?
backHtml: Neonatal: under 28 days. Postneonatal: 28 days to under 1 year.

frontHtml: Denominator of the maternal mortality ratio?
backHtml: 100,000 live births.

frontHtml: How much does a death after the cut-off age add to YPLL?
backHtml: Zero (never a negative number).

frontHtml: Managing medications, money and shopping belong to which functional domain?
backHtml: Instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs).

frontHtml: Does self-rated health predict mortality after adjusting for diagnosed disease?
backHtml: Yes; it is an independent predictor of mortality and decline.

frontHtml: How is median survival read from a Kaplan-Meier curve?
backHtml: The earliest time at which the curve reaches or falls below 0.5.

frontHtml: What do tick marks on a Kaplan-Meier curve show?
backHtml: Censored participants (left follow-up event-free); the curve does not drop at a tick.

frontHtml: Which test compares two Kaplan-Meier curves over the whole follow-up?
backHtml: The log-rank test.

frontHtml: Hazard ratio 0.70: what does it mean?
backHtml: At any time, a 30% lower event rate among those still at risk.

frontHtml: What does informative censoring of the sickest patients do to a Kaplan-Meier estimate?
backHtml: It overestimates survival.

frontHtml: Crossing survival curves violate which Cox model assumption?
backHtml: Proportional hazards.

frontHtml: DALY formula?
backHtml: DALY = YLL + YLD.

frontHtml: QALY formula?
backHtml: Years lived × utility (0 = dead, 1 = full health).

frontHtml: ICER formula?
backHtml: (Cost new − cost old) ÷ (QALYs new − QALYs old).

frontHtml: Attributable risk percent in the exposed, in terms of RR?
backHtml: (RR − 1) ÷ RR.

frontHtml: Population attributable fraction formula?
backHtml: P<sub>e</sub>(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + P<sub>e</sub>(RR − 1)].

frontHtml: Which measure tells a health department how many community cases an exposure causes?
backHtml: Population attributable risk.

frontHtml: Is an NNT rounded up or down?
backHtml: Up, to the next whole person.

frontHtml: Expansive pyramid: what birth and death rates?
backHtml: High birth rate with high (or recently falling) death rate; rapid growth.

frontHtml: Constrictive pyramid: what does the narrow base mean?
backHtml: Fertility below replacement; the population is ageing and may shrink.

frontHtml: Total dependency ratio formula?
Which demographic transition stage has falling death rates but high birth rates?
backHtml: Stage 2: rapid population growth.

frontHtml: Population ageing with unchanged age-specific risk: effect on crude prevalence of dementia?
backHtml: Crude prevalence rises; age-specific and age-adjusted rates are unchanged.

frontHtml: A one-sex bulge in working ages on a pyramid suggests what?
backHtml: Labour migration.

frontHtml: Passive vs active surveillance?
backHtml: Passive: providers report on their own. Active: the health department seeks out cases.

frontHtml: Epidemic vs endemic?
backHtml: Endemic: usual level. Epidemic: clearly in excess of the usual level.

frontHtml: What must a case definition never include?
backHtml: The exposure under investigation.

frontHtml: Epidemic curve with one sharp peak?
backHtml: Point-source outbreak.

frontHtml: Epidemic curve with regularly spaced, growing waves?
backHtml: Propagated (person-to-person) outbreak.

frontHtml: Analytic design for a closed group outbreak vs a dispersed community outbreak?
backHtml: Closed group: retrospective cohort. Community: case-control.

frontHtml: How is the likely vehicle identified in a food-specific attack rate table?
backHtml: High attack rate in eaters, low in non-eaters (large ratio), explaining most cases.

frontHtml: Herd immunity threshold formula?
Vaccination coverage needed for herd immunity with an imperfect vaccine?
backHtml: (1 − 1/R<sub>0</sub>) ÷ vaccine effectiveness.

frontHtml: R<sub>0</sub> vs R<sub>t</sub>: which falls as immunity rises?
backHtml: R<sub>t</sub> (effective reproduction number).

frontHtml: Latent period shorter than incubation period implies what?
backHtml: Presymptomatic transmission.

frontHtml: Isolation vs quarantine?
backHtml: Isolation: the ill or infected. Quarantine: exposed people who are well.

frontHtml: Which infections need airborne precautions?
backHtml: Measles, varicella or disseminated zoster, pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis.

frontHtml: Why soap and water for C. difficile?
backHtml: Alcohol does not kill its spores.

frontHtml: Primordial prevention aims to do what?
backHtml: Prevent risk factors from emerging, through social and environmental conditions.

frontHtml: Screening asymptomatic people is which level of prevention?
backHtml: Secondary prevention.

frontHtml: Cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction is which level of prevention?
backHtml: Tertiary prevention.

frontHtml: What is quaternary prevention?
backHtml: Protecting people from overmedicalisation and harm from unnecessary care.

frontHtml: What is the prevention paradox?
backHtml: Many people at modest risk produce more cases than few at high risk, so population-wide shifts prevent the most disease.

frontHtml: Which outcome is free of lead-time and overdiagnosis bias when judging screening?
backHtml: Disease-specific mortality in the whole screened vs unscreened population.

frontHtml: Post-exposure prophylaxis is which level of prevention?
backHtml: Primary prevention (it stops infection from becoming disease).

frontHtml: How are central line infections compared between ICUs?
backHtml: Infections per 1,000 central line-days.

frontHtml: A new looser diagnostic threshold: effect on recorded incidence and prevalence?
backHtml: Both rise.

frontHtml: Rise in postneonatal mortality from sudden sleep-related deaths: best intervention?
backHtml: Safe infant sleep education.

frontHtml: Small county, infant deaths 3 → 6 in a year: next step?
backHtml: Pool several years and review each death; small numbers vary by chance.

frontHtml: Outcome measure for how a programme changes daily life?
backHtml: A validated patient-reported function or quality-of-life measure.

frontHtml: Conditional survival from time a to b?
backHtml: S(b) ÷ S(a).

frontHtml: A flat tail with few patients at risk: what can you conclude?
backHtml: Little: the estimate is imprecise and cannot prove cure.

frontHtml: How should median survival be explained to a patient?
backHtml: Half of the study patients were alive at that time; it is not an individual prediction.

frontHtml: Strategy costs more and yields fewer QALYs than another: term?
backHtml: Dominated; drop it.

frontHtml: NNH formula?
backHtml: 1 ÷ absolute risk increase, for a stated time.

frontHtml: Patient asks you not to report a notifiable disease: what do you do?
backHtml: Report it and explain why; public health reporting needs no consent under HIPAA.

frontHtml: First step after a syndromic surveillance alarm?
backHtml: Verify the signal (review records, contact clinicians).

frontHtml: Best case definition early in an outbreak?
backHtml: Broad and sensitive (clinical criteria + person, place, time).

frontHtml: When should control measures start in an outbreak?
backHtml: As soon as a likely source is identified, in parallel with the investigation.

frontHtml: Case rise starting when a new PCR panel was introduced, no clustering?
backHtml: Likely a detection artefact (pseudo-outbreak).

frontHtml: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis on admission: precautions?
backHtml: Airborne infection isolation room and N95 respirators, started on suspicion.

frontHtml: Susceptible child exposed to measles 2 days ago: management?
backHtml: MMR vaccine now (within 72 hours).

frontHtml: Newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother: management?
backHtml: Hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth.

frontHtml: Who receives chemoprophylaxis after a case of meningococcal disease?
backHtml: Close contacts (household, roommates, those exposed to oral secretions).

frontHtml: R<sub>t</sub> falls to 0.8: meaning?
backHtml: Each case infects fewer than one other person on average; cases decline gradually.

frontHtml: Crude cancer incidence rises, age-adjusted flat: conclusion?
backHtml: Population ageing; plan capacity rather than investigate a cluster.

frontHtml: How should future disease caseload be projected?
backHtml: Apply age-specific rates to the projected age structure.

frontHtml: Evidence-based falls prevention for older adults at increased risk?
backHtml: Exercise programmes for gait, balance and strength.

frontHtml: Acute low back pain without red flags: imaging?
backHtml: No; explain why and offer a recovery plan.

frontHtml: Bat found in the room of a sleeping person, bat unavailable: management?
backHtml: Rabies immune globulin plus rabies vaccine series.

frontHtml: Screening for ovarian cancer in average-risk women?
backHtml: Not recommended (no mortality benefit, harms from false positives).

frontHtml: Indirect standardisation result: observed 45, expected 30. Interpretation?
backHtml: SMR 1.5: 50% more deaths than expected for the group's age and sex structure.

frontHtml: Survival curves that cross: what summary should you report?
backHtml: Time-specific results (early mortality, later survival), not one hazard ratio.

frontHtml: Exposure X: 1% prevalence, RR 10. Exposure Y: 40% prevalence, RR 2. Which causes more cases?
backHtml: Exposure Y (PAR% about 29% vs 8%).

frontHtml: Food that the most ill people ate but nearly everyone ate: likely vehicle?
backHtml: Not necessarily; compare attack rates in eaters and non-eaters.

frontHtml: Screening raised 5-year survival but not the death rate: conclusion?
backHtml: Lead time and overdiagnosis; no evidence of lives saved.

frontHtml: Herd immunity coverage with R<sub>0</sub> 4 and a 95% effective vaccine?
What distinguishes a case series from a case report?
backHtml: A case series describes several patients with a shared condition or exposure; a case report describes one.

frontHtml: What is the main scientific use of a case report or case series?
backHtml: Generating a hypothesis (a signal) to be tested by an analytical study.

frontHtml: Why can a case series not estimate incidence?
backHtml: It has cases (a numerator) but no population at risk (a denominator).

frontHtml: What is the main limitation of a case series for causal inference?
backHtml: No comparison group.

frontHtml: What is the key weakness of spontaneous adverse-event reporting?
backHtml: Under-reporting and no denominator, so risk cannot be estimated from reports alone.

frontHtml: Ecological vs cross-sectional: what is the difference in unit of analysis?
backHtml: Ecological = groups (countries, counties); cross-sectional = individuals at one time point.

frontHtml: Case-control studies select participants by what?
backHtml: By outcome (cases with disease, controls without), then look back at exposure.

frontHtml: What measure of association does a case-control study give?
backHtml: The odds ratio, (a × d)/(b × c).

frontHtml: A case-control study of a rare disease reports an odds ratio of 3. How can that figure be read?
backHtml: As roughly a threefold risk: with a rare outcome, the odds ratio closely tracks the relative risk.

frontHtml: Which design suits a rare exposure with several possible outcomes?
backHtml: A cohort study.

frontHtml: What makes a cohort study retrospective (historical)?
backHtml: Exposure and outcomes are reconstructed from existing records; selection is still by exposure.

frontHtml: What is a nested case-control study?
backHtml: Cases and controls sampled from within a cohort whose exposure data or samples were collected at baseline.

frontHtml: Which design compares each case's exposure just before an acute event with his or her own earlier exposure?
backHtml: Case-crossover study.

frontHtml: What is the ecological fallacy?
backHtml: Assuming a group-level association holds for the individuals within the groups.

frontHtml: What is the purpose of a washout period in a crossover trial?
backHtml: To prevent carryover of the first treatment's effect into the second period.

frontHtml: What is a 2 × 2 factorial trial?
backHtml: Randomization to two interventions at once, giving four groups, so each intervention is tested in one trial.

frontHtml: Why randomize clusters (schools, clinics) instead of individuals?
backHtml: Group-level delivery or contamination between individuals; the cost is lower power.

frontHtml: Design effect formula for a cluster design?
backHtml: 1 + (m − 1) × ICC, where m = mean cluster size and ICC = intracluster correlation.

frontHtml: When is a new treatment non-inferior?
backHtml: When the whole confidence interval for the difference lies on the acceptable side of the prespecified margin.

frontHtml: Explanatory vs pragmatic trial?
backHtml: Explanatory: can it work under ideal conditions (efficacy). Pragmatic: does it work in usual care (effectiveness).

frontHtml: Main goals of a phase 1 study?
backHtml: Safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and dose finding in a small number of people.

frontHtml: Systematic review vs meta-analysis?
backHtml: Systematic review = explicit, reproducible search, selection and appraisal; meta-analysis = statistical pooling of the results.

frontHtml: On a forest plot, what does the size of a study's square show?
backHtml: Its weight in the pooled estimate (larger = more precise).

frontHtml: When is a pooled result on a forest plot statistically significant?
backHtml: When the diamond does not touch the line of no effect (1 for ratios, 0 for differences).

frontHtml: What does I² estimate?
backHtml: The percentage of variation between study results due to real heterogeneity rather than chance.

frontHtml: Random effects vs fixed effect when heterogeneity is present?
backHtml: Random effects gives a wider confidence interval and more even weights.

frontHtml: What does an asymmetric funnel plot with missing small null studies suggest?
backHtml: Publication bias or other small-study effects; the pooled effect is probably overstated.

frontHtml: Stratified vs cluster sampling?
backHtml: Stratified = random sample from every subgroup; cluster = random selection of some whole groups.

frontHtml: What is a sampling frame?
backHtml: The list or mechanism from which the sample is actually drawn.

frontHtml: What does allocation concealment prevent?
backHtml: Selection bias at enrolment (recruiters cannot foresee or influence the next assignment).

frontHtml: Main advantage of block randomization?
backHtml: Keeps group sizes nearly equal throughout enrolment.

frontHtml: Why use stratified randomization?
backHtml: To guarantee balance between arms on a few strong prognostic factors, especially in small trials.

frontHtml: What is overmatching, and its effect?
backHtml: Matching on a factor linked to the exposure or on its causal path; biases the OR toward 1.

frontHtml: Ideal source of controls in a case-control study?
backHtml: The same source population that produced the cases.

frontHtml: Intention-to-treat analysis analyses participants how?
backHtml: All randomized participants, in the group to which they were assigned.

frontHtml: Why is intention-to-treat the primary analysis of superiority trials?
backHtml: It preserves the comparability created by randomization.

frontHtml: Per-protocol vs as-treated analysis?
backHtml: Per-protocol: only protocol-adherent participants. As-treated: everyone regrouped by treatment actually received.

frontHtml: Effect of crossover or contamination on an ITT estimate?
backHtml: Bias toward the null (smaller apparent effect).

frontHtml: Main disadvantage of a run-in period?
backHtml: Reduced generalizability: results apply to adherent, tolerant patients.

frontHtml: Why is LOCF biased in a progressive disease?
backHtml: It freezes scores at dropout, ignoring further decline, which flatters the arm with earlier dropouts.

frontHtml: Why do non-inferiority trials report per-protocol as well as ITT?
backHtml: Dilution in ITT makes arms look alike, favouring a false non-inferiority claim.

frontHtml: When does a research question call for qualitative methods?
backHtml: When it asks why or how, about experiences or processes whose key factors are not yet known.

frontHtml: What is data saturation?
backHtml: The point at which new interviews or observations produce no new themes.

frontHtml: What is snowball sampling used for?
backHtml: Reaching hidden populations without a sampling frame, by having participants recruit others.

frontHtml: What is triangulation?
backHtml: Cross-checking findings across several data sources, methods or researchers.

frontHtml: What is reflexivity?
backHtml: The researcher's explicit examination of how his or her own background shapes the study.

frontHtml: Which strategy supports transferability?
backHtml: Thick description of the setting and participants.

frontHtml: A clinician suspects a new adverse drug reaction. Next step?
backHtml: Report it to the regulator's adverse-event reporting program; proof of causation is not required.

frontHtml: What must you obtain before publishing a case report?
backHtml: The patient's written consent for publication, with identifying details minimised.

frontHtml: Rare disease, several suspected exposures: which design?
backHtml: Case-control.

frontHtml: "How many of my patients have this now?": which design?
backHtml: Cross-sectional survey (prevalence).

frontHtml: Dependent vs independent variable?
backHtml: Dependent = outcome; independent = exposure, predictor or intervention.

frontHtml: Effective treatment exists and withholding it risks serious harm: what comparator?
backHtml: An active control (current standard treatment).

frontHtml: Non-inferiority confidence interval crosses the margin and includes 0: conclusion?
backHtml: Inconclusive: neither non-inferiority nor inferiority shown.

frontHtml: Which estimate predicts the effect of prescribing a drug to a clinic population?
backHtml: The intention-to-treat estimate.

frontHtml: Adherence predicts better survival in the placebo arm too. What does that mean?
backHtml: Healthy-adherer effect: adherence marks better prognosis, not drug benefit.

frontHtml: What is the therapeutic misconception?
backHtml: Believing that a research study is designed to benefit the participant personally.

frontHtml: How do you convert a pooled RR into an NNT for your patients?
backHtml: ARR = baseline risk × (1 − RR); NNT = 1/ARR.

frontHtml: Low I²: what does it show and not show?
backHtml: Results are consistent; it does not show they are free of bias.

frontHtml: What is a risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis?
backHtml: Repeating the meta-analysis using only trials at low risk of bias to see if the result holds.

frontHtml: Does pooling many cohort studies remove confounding?
backHtml: No. It increases precision, not validity.

frontHtml: Below about how many studies is a funnel plot unreliable?
backHtml: About ten.

frontHtml: No list of individuals, but a list of villages; travel is costly. Sampling approach?
backHtml: Cluster sampling.

frontHtml: A patient falls outside a trial's eligibility criteria. What does the trial tell you about her?
backHtml: Nothing direct: benefit and harm are uncertain, not proven absent.

frontHtml: Day-of-the-week allocation: what is the problem?
backHtml: It is predictable, so it cannot be concealed and invites selection bias.

frontHtml: Before-after improvement in people enrolled for an extreme value: main alternative explanation?
backHtml: Regression to the mean (a concurrent control group is needed).

frontHtml: Does a bigger convenience sample reduce selection bias?
backHtml: No. It increases precision only.

frontHtml: Sensitive topic such as intimate partner violence: focus groups or individual interviews?
backHtml: Individual in-depth interviews in a private, safe setting.

frontHtml: Sampling to capture a wide range of experiences in an interview study?
backHtml: Purposive (maximum-variation) sampling.

frontHtml: What is member checking?
backHtml: Returning findings to participants to confirm they reflect their experiences (supports credibility).

frontHtml: Can a qualitative study estimate how common a reason is?
backHtml: No. It shows the range of reasons, not their frequency.

frontHtml: Survey to measure a problem plus interviews to explain it, integrated: which design?
backHtml: Mixed methods.

frontHtml: Equivalence margins ±5; 95% CI −1 to +7. Conclusion?
backHtml: Non-inferior (lower limit above −5) but not equivalent (upper limit above +5) and not superior (includes 0).

frontHtml: Forest plot: every trial's CI crosses 1 but the diamond does not. Conclusion?
backHtml: The pooled evidence shows a statistically significant effect.

frontHtml: ITT risk difference when drug arm events = 35/500 and placebo arm = 47/500?
backHtml: 9.4% − 7.0% = 2.4 percentage points.

frontHtml: Pooled RR 0.75 and baseline risk 20%: NNT?
Non-inferiority CI −12.0 to 1.0 with a −10 margin?
backHtml: Inconclusive.

frontHtml: Cohort: 48/400 exposed vs 120/1,600 unexposed. Relative risk?
From a cohort 2×2 table, what is the relative risk formula?
backHtml: RR = [a ÷ (a + b)] ÷ [c ÷ (c + d)], each row's cases over that row's total.

frontHtml: How is the relative risk reduction related to the relative risk?
backHtml: RRR = 1 − RR (e.g. RR 0.75 → RRR 25%).

frontHtml: What is the number needed to treat?
backHtml: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction, over the trial's time frame, rounded up.

frontHtml: Control risk 12%, treated risk 9%: what is the NNT?
A 95% CI for a relative risk includes 1. What does that mean?
backHtml: The association is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

frontHtml: Same RRR, higher baseline risk: what happens to ARR and NNT?
backHtml: ARR rises and NNT falls (ARR = baseline risk × RRR).

frontHtml: What is the odds ratio formula for a 2×2 table?
backHtml: OR = (a × d) ÷ (b × c).

frontHtml: Why can't a case-control study give a relative risk directly?
backHtml: Investigators fix the numbers of cases and controls, so outcome risk in each exposure group is not observed.

frontHtml: When does the odds ratio approximate the relative risk?
backHtml: When the outcome is rare (roughly under 10%) in the groups compared.

frontHtml: For a common outcome, is the OR closer to or farther from 1 than the RR?
backHtml: Farther from 1: it overstates the strength of the association.

frontHtml: What is a hazard ratio?
backHtml: The ratio of instantaneous event rates between groups over follow-up, from time-to-event (e.g. Cox) analysis.

frontHtml: What does an exponentiated logistic regression coefficient represent?
backHtml: An adjusted odds ratio for that predictor, other variables held constant.

frontHtml: What is attributable risk percent among the exposed?
backHtml: (Risk exposed − risk unexposed) ÷ risk exposed = (RR − 1) ÷ RR.

frontHtml: What is the population attributable fraction formula?
backHtml: PAF = p(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + p(RR − 1)], with p = proportion exposed.

frontHtml: Follow-up time varies between people. Which measure compares groups?
backHtml: Incidence rate ratio: events per person-time in each group.

frontHtml: Which ratio measure comes from a cross-sectional survey?
backHtml: The prevalence ratio (or prevalence odds ratio).

frontHtml: What is the positive likelihood ratio?
backHtml: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity).

frontHtml: Which measures cannot be calculated directly from a case-control study?
backHtml: Incidence, relative risk and attributable risk.

frontHtml: In a positively (right) skewed distribution, what is the order of mean, median and mode?
backHtml: Mode < median < mean.

frontHtml: What proportions of a normal distribution lie within ±1, ±2 and ±3 SD?
What is the standard error of the mean?
backHtml: SEM = SD ÷ √n; it measures the precision of the sample mean.

frontHtml: What is a z-score?
backHtml: (Value − mean) ÷ SD: the number of SDs from the mean.

frontHtml: Which scale has ordered categories with unequal steps?
backHtml: Ordinal (e.g. tumour grade 1–3).

frontHtml: What is regression to the mean?
backHtml: Extreme first measurements tend to be followed by values closer to the average, even without intervention.

frontHtml: Which measure of centre resists outliers?
backHtml: The median.

frontHtml: What determines the strength of a Pearson correlation?
backHtml: Its absolute value |r|; the sign gives only direction.

frontHtml: What does r² represent?
backHtml: The proportion of variance in one variable explained by its linear relation with the other.

frontHtml: When is Spearman rank correlation preferred?
backHtml: Ordinal data, outliers, skewed data or monotonic non-linear relations.

frontHtml: In y = a + bx, what does b mean?
backHtml: The slope: change in y for each one-unit increase in x.

frontHtml: Which test compares two categorical variables?
backHtml: Chi-square (Fisher's exact test when expected counts are small).

frontHtml: Which test compares means of three or more groups?
backHtml: Analysis of variance (ANOVA).

frontHtml: Can a strong relationship give r ≈ 0?
backHtml: Yes, if it is non-linear (e.g. U-shaped).

frontHtml: Which disease features justify screening?
backHtml: Important burden, a detectable preclinical phase and better outcomes with early treatment.

frontHtml: Reliability versus validity?
backHtml: Reliability = repeat measurements agree (precision); validity = measurements match the truth (accuracy).

frontHtml: What does kappa measure?
backHtml: Agreement between raters beyond that expected by chance: (p<sub>o</sub> − p<sub>e</sub>) ÷ (1 − p<sub>e</sub>).

frontHtml: Serial testing (both must be positive): effect on sensitivity and specificity?
backHtml: Sensitivity falls, specificity rises.

frontHtml: Parallel testing (either positive): effect on sensitivity and specificity?
backHtml: Sensitivity rises, specificity falls.

frontHtml: What pattern after screening suggests overdiagnosis?
backHtml: Early-stage incidence rises while late-stage incidence and mortality do not fall.

frontHtml: What is sensitivity?
backHtml: TP ÷ (TP + FN): the proportion of diseased people who test positive.

frontHtml: What is specificity?
backHtml: TN ÷ (TN + FP): the proportion of non-diseased people who test negative.

frontHtml: What is the positive predictive value?
backHtml: TP ÷ (TP + FP): the probability of disease given a positive test.

frontHtml: As prevalence falls, what happens to PPV and NPV?
backHtml: PPV falls, NPV rises; sensitivity and specificity are unchanged.

frontHtml: Which property makes a negative result good at ruling disease out?
backHtml: High sensitivity (few false negatives).

frontHtml: Lowering a test's positive cut-off does what?
backHtml: Raises sensitivity and lowers specificity.

frontHtml: What are the axes of an ROC curve?
backHtml: Sensitivity (y) against 1 − specificity (x).

frontHtml: What AUC indicates no discrimination?
backHtml: 0.5 (the diagonal).

frontHtml: What does the AUC mean as a probability?
backHtml: The chance that a random diseased person has a more abnormal value than a random non-diseased person.

frontHtml: Does prevalence change the ROC curve?
backHtml: No; it changes predictive values, not sensitivity or specificity.

frontHtml: With equal error costs, which ROC point is best?
backHtml: The point farthest from the diagonal (maximum Youden index, sens + spec − 1).

frontHtml: An ROC curve lies below the diagonal (AUC 0.3). What does it mean?
backHtml: The positivity rule is reversed; flipping it gives AUC 0.7.

frontHtml: P(A and B) for independent events?
backHtml: P(A) × P(B).

frontHtml: P(A or B) for mutually exclusive events?
backHtml: P(A) + P(B).

frontHtml: Probability of at least one event in n independent trials, each p?
backHtml: 1 − (1 − p)<sup>n</sup>.

frontHtml: How do you get post-test probability from a likelihood ratio?
backHtml: Probability → odds, × LR, odds → probability.

frontHtml: Convert a probability of 0.2 to odds.
In a conditional probability P(A | B), which group forms the denominator?
backHtml: Only those meeting the condition B: divide the count with both A and B by the count with B.

frontHtml: How do you estimate an individual patient's ARR from a trial?
backHtml: Patient's baseline risk × the trial's relative risk reduction.

frontHtml: Best format for explaining a treatment effect to a patient?
backHtml: Absolute numbers as natural frequencies with a time frame (e.g. 3 fewer in 100 over 5 years).

frontHtml: What is the number needed to harm?
backHtml: 1 ÷ absolute risk increase.

frontHtml: An RR of 1.0 with a wide CI: what can you tell the patient?
backHtml: The study found no difference but cannot exclude a meaningful effect.

frontHtml: Why compare NNT and NNH over the same time frame?
backHtml: So benefit and harm are weighed on the same scale.

frontHtml: Vaccine effectiveness from a case-control (test-negative) study?
Crude OR 2.8 falls to adjusted OR 1.9 (CI excludes 1). Interpretation?
backHtml: Confounding explained part of the association; an independent association remains.

frontHtml: How do you judge whether a subgroup's effect differs from the overall effect?
backHtml: By the test for interaction, not by whether the subgroup CI crosses 1.

frontHtml: What do you need besides an HR to get an NNT?
backHtml: Absolute event proportions (e.g. Kaplan-Meier estimates at a time point).

frontHtml: Can an adjusted OR for a common outcome be read as "times as likely"?
backHtml: No; it overstates the relative risk.

frontHtml: How should infection rates be compared between hospital units?
backHtml: Per device-days (e.g. per 1,000 central line-days), not by counts.

frontHtml: Which measure guides which risk factor to target in a population?
backHtml: The population attributable fraction (combines prevalence and RR).

frontHtml: Excess cases among the exposed from a baseline rate and RR?
backHtml: Baseline rate × (RR − 1).

frontHtml: A finding has high sensitivity but LR+ near 1. Is its presence useful?
backHtml: Little; its absence (low LR−) is more useful.

frontHtml: Rate 2 vs 5 per 10,000 person-years: what is the excess rate?
backHtml: 3 per 10,000 person-years.

frontHtml: What share of healthy people fall above a 95% reference interval?
backHtml: About 2.5% (5% outside in both tails).

frontHtml: How do you convert a reported SEM back to the SD?
backHtml: SD = SEM × √n.

frontHtml: Which summary best describes typical cost when a few cases are very expensive?
backHtml: The median (with IQR).

frontHtml: Which model for a yes/no outcome with several predictors?
backHtml: Multiple logistic regression (adjusted odds ratios).

frontHtml: Which model for time to event with censoring and covariates?
backHtml: Cox proportional hazards regression.

frontHtml: How should agreement between two measurement methods be assessed?
backHtml: With a difference (Bland-Altman) analysis, not correlation.

frontHtml: What is the ecological fallacy?
backHtml: Applying a group-level association to individuals.

frontHtml: When should you discuss stopping screening in an older patient?
backHtml: When life expectancy is shorter than the time screening takes to give benefit.

frontHtml: What outcome shows a screening programme truly works?
backHtml: Lower mortality (or morbidity) in randomized comparisons.

frontHtml: How is a reactive screening test described to the patient?
backHtml: As a result that needs confirmatory testing, not a diagnosis.

frontHtml: Systems response to low inter-rater kappa?
backHtml: Standardise criteria, train with reference cases, add consensus review and re-audit.

frontHtml: A test moves from a referral centre to primary care. What changes?
backHtml: PPV falls and NPV rises; sensitivity and specificity stay similar.

frontHtml: Which ROC region suits a rule-out strategy?
backHtml: High sensitivity (upper right of the curve).

frontHtml: Which ROC region suits confirming before hazardous treatment?
backHtml: High specificity (lower left of the curve).

frontHtml: What is spectrum bias in a diagnostic study?
backHtml: Inflated accuracy from comparing clear-cut cases with healthy controls.

frontHtml: Two ROC curves cross. How do you choose?
backHtml: Compare them within the range of false-positive rates acceptable for the use.

frontHtml: When is a diagnostic test not worth ordering?
backHtml: When no plausible result could move the probability across a decision threshold.

frontHtml: Pre-test probability 20%, LR 10: post-test probability?
Above the treatment threshold, what do you do?
backHtml: Treat without further testing.

frontHtml: Best way to explain a post-test probability to a patient?
backHtml: Natural frequencies (e.g. 30 of 1,000 people with this result have the condition).

frontHtml: Cumulative probability of at least one failure over n independent years?
backHtml: 1 − (1 − p)<sup>n</sup>.

frontHtml: A scatter plot shows a clear U shape. What is Pearson r likely to be?
backHtml: Close to 0, because r measures only linear association.

frontHtml: Two tests (90/80 and 80/90 sens/spec) used in series: combined values?
backHtml: Sensitivity 72%, specificity 98%.

frontHtml: Sens 99.8%, spec 99.5%, prevalence 0.2%: PPV?
backHtml: About 29%: most reactive results are false positives.

frontHtml: Reactive HIV antigen/antibody screen, negative differentiation assay: next step?
backHtml: HIV-1 nucleic acid test.

frontHtml: Crossing ROC curves and a maximum false-positive rate of 5%: which test?
backHtml: The one with higher sensitivity in that low false-positive region, even if its AUC is lower.

frontHtml: First step when a patient asks for an unproven screening test?
backHtml: Explore what prompted the request, then explain benefits and harms.

frontHtml: New meter vs lab: r = 0.98, slope 1.15. Do they agree?
backHtml: No: the meter reads about 15% higher; use a difference analysis.

frontHtml: Which causal consideration is the only one that must be satisfied?
backHtml: Temporality: the exposure must precede the outcome.

frontHtml: What are the four alternative explanations to check before calling an association causal?
backHtml: Chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation.

frontHtml: Risk rising steadily with dose or duration of exposure illustrates which causal consideration?
backHtml: Biological gradient (dose-response).

frontHtml: Disease incidence falls after an exposure is removed. Which causal consideration does this support?
backHtml: Experiment (reversibility).

frontHtml: Why are cross-sectional studies especially prone to reverse causation?
backHtml: Exposure and outcome are measured at the same time, so temporality cannot be established.

frontHtml: What is protopathic bias?
backHtml: Early symptoms of an undiagnosed disease prompt the exposure (for example, a remedy), making the exposure look like a cause.

frontHtml: Which causal consideration is usually regarded as the weakest?
backHtml: Specificity: most causes have several effects.

frontHtml: What does a P value of 0.04 mean?
backHtml: If there were truly no effect, results at least this extreme would occur about 4% of the time.

frontHtml: Define a type I error.
backHtml: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive); its probability is alpha.

frontHtml: Define a type II error.
backHtml: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative); its probability is beta.

frontHtml: What is statistical power?
backHtml: The chance that a study finds a real effect of a stated size; it equals 1 − β.

frontHtml: Name four things that increase power.
backHtml: Larger sample, larger true effect, less variability, higher alpha.

frontHtml: A 95% CI for a ratio includes 1. What does this imply about P?
backHtml: P > 0.05 (not significant at the 0.05 level).

frontHtml: Chance of at least one false positive with k independent tests at alpha 0.05?
backHtml: 1 − 0.95<sup>k</sup> (about 64% for 20 tests).

frontHtml: Which test compares a continuous outcome measured before and after in the same people?
backHtml: Paired t-test.

frontHtml: In a box plot, what do the box and the line inside it show?
backHtml: The interquartile range (middle 50%) and the median.

frontHtml: How do you read median survival from a Kaplan-Meier curve?
backHtml: The time at which the curve first falls to 0.50.

frontHtml: Convert an SEM to an SD.
backHtml: SD = SEM × √n (for example, SEM 3 with n = 25 gives SD 15).

frontHtml: In a forest plot, what does the size of each square represent?
backHtml: The study's weight, mainly its precision.

frontHtml: Why can a pooled meta-analysis estimate be significant when most individual trials are not?
backHtml: Pooling combines information, narrowing the confidence interval.

frontHtml: What visual trick makes small differences between bars look large?
backHtml: A truncated y-axis that does not start at zero.

frontHtml: What is Berkson bias?
backHtml: A spurious association in hospital-based studies because exposure and disease both raise the chance of admission.

frontHtml: Non-differential misclassification of a binary exposure usually biases results in which direction?
backHtml: Toward the null (RR or OR toward 1).

frontHtml: What is the Hawthorne effect?
backHtml: Participants change their behaviour because they know they are being observed.

frontHtml: How does lead-time bias inflate screening results?
backHtml: Earlier diagnosis lengthens measured survival without delaying death.

frontHtml: What is length-time bias?
backHtml: Periodic screening preferentially detects slow-growing disease with a better prognosis.

frontHtml: Stratum-specific estimates agree with each other but differ from the crude estimate. What is present?
backHtml: Confounding: adjust for the third variable.

frontHtml: Stratum-specific estimates differ from each other. What is present?
backHtml: Effect modification: report each stratum separately.

frontHtml: Which method controls both measured and unmeasured confounders?
backHtml: Randomization.

frontHtml: Define internal validity.
backHtml: Whether a study got the right answer for the people it enrolled, without bias or confounding distorting it.

frontHtml: Define external validity.
backHtml: The degree to which a study's result applies to other people, settings and times (generalizability).

frontHtml: Efficacy versus effectiveness?
backHtml: Efficacy: effect under ideal trial conditions. Effectiveness: effect in routine practice (usually smaller).

frontHtml: Random sampling protects which kind of validity?
backHtml: External validity (a representative sample).

frontHtml: Random allocation protects which kind of validity?
backHtml: Internal validity (comparable groups).

frontHtml: Name two trial features that commonly limit external validity.
backHtml: Strict exclusion criteria and placebo run-in periods (also expert single-centre settings).

frontHtml: What is the minimal clinically important difference?
backHtml: The smallest change in an outcome that patients would notice as a benefit and that would justify a change in treatment.

frontHtml: Can a trivial effect be statistically significant?
backHtml: Yes: very large samples detect very small differences.

frontHtml: What is a surrogate end point?
backHtml: A biomarker or physiological measure used in place of an outcome patients experience.

frontHtml: Main advantage of a composite end point?
backHtml: More events, so more power with fewer participants.

frontHtml: Main caution when reading a composite end point?
backHtml: A single, often less serious, component may drive the result.

frontHtml: What weight should a significant secondary outcome get when the primary end point is negative?
backHtml: Hypothesis-generating only.

frontHtml: How do you calculate a patient-specific ARR?
backHtml: Patient's baseline risk × the trial's relative risk reduction.

frontHtml: A trial reports a relative risk reduction of 30%. How do you estimate the absolute benefit for your own patient?
backHtml: Multiply the patient's own baseline risk by the RRR (e.g. 25% × 0.20 = 5 points, so NNT = 20).

frontHtml: Define the number needed to harm.
backHtml: 1 / absolute risk increase for an adverse outcome.

frontHtml: What is the best format for communicating risk to patients?
backHtml: Absolute numbers as natural frequencies with a common denominator and time frame.

frontHtml: RRR 25%, baseline risk 4%: what is the NNT?
backHtml: ARR = 1%, so NNT = 100.

frontHtml: In which order should you read an abstract item?
backHtml: Questions first, then objective, design, participants, outcomes, results, and finally the conclusion.

frontHtml: A non-significant superiority trial concludes the drugs are 'equally effective'. Is that supported?
backHtml: No: equivalence needs a prespecified margin and a CI within it.

frontHtml: Survival after diagnosis rose after a screening programme. Is that evidence of benefit?
backHtml: No: judge screening by population disease-specific mortality.

frontHtml: A before-after QI comparison shows improvement. What should you check first?
backHtml: Whether the outcome was already trending the same way before the intervention.

frontHtml: An observational abstract says 'X prevents Y'. What is wrong?
backHtml: Causal language from an association; consider confounding, bias and reverse causation.

frontHtml: Zero serious events in n patients: approximate upper 95% limit of the true rate?
backHtml: About 3 / n (rule of three).

frontHtml: Why is intention-to-treat analysis primary in superiority trials?
backHtml: It preserves randomization; per-protocol results can be biased by unequal dropout.

frontHtml: Crude HR 0.6 becomes 1.0 after adjustment for exercise and smoking. Interpretation?
backHtml: Confounding (a healthy-user effect); no evidence of benefit.

frontHtml: A wide CI includes both no effect and important benefit. What should you tell a patient?
backHtml: The study is inconclusive, not negative.

frontHtml: Does a larger sample reduce bias?
backHtml: No: it reduces random error only; bias persists.

frontHtml: Your patient would have been excluded from the trial. What does that mean for its results?
backHtml: They may not apply; benefit and harm for this patient are uncertain.

frontHtml: Effect is significant, but the whole CI lies below the MCID. Conclusion?
backHtml: Statistically but not clinically significant.

frontHtml: Why does a placebo run-in inflate apparent benefit?
backHtml: It removes placebo responders and non-adherent people, so participants are unlike routine patients.

frontHtml: Which trial type best informs a health-system decision about usual care?
backHtml: A pragmatic trial in similar settings (effectiveness).

frontHtml: A drug improves a surrogate end point. What do you need before claiming clinical benefit?
backHtml: An adequately powered trial showing improvement in the patient-important outcome.

frontHtml: Baseline 10-year risk 15%, RRR 20%: ARR and NNT?
backHtml: ARR 3%; NNT 34 (33.3 rounded up).

frontHtml: How should benefit and harm be presented together?
backHtml: As natural frequencies with the same denominator and time frame.

frontHtml: Name two poor responses to a patient asking about a headline study.
backHtml: Simply agreeing with the headline, or dismissing the question.

frontHtml: Is departing from a guideline ever appropriate?
backHtml: Yes, for a patient unlike the evidence base or with different values, with reasoning explained and documented.

frontHtml: Why do low-risk patients gain little from an impressive RRR?
backHtml: Absolute benefit = baseline risk × RRR, so it is small when baseline risk is low.

frontHtml: A screening programme doubles diagnoses while disease-specific deaths stay flat. What does that suggest?
backHtml: Overdiagnosis, not benefit.

frontHtml: A composite benefit comes almost entirely from fewer urgent revascularizations. What should the conclusion say?
backHtml: Benefit is in that component; no clear effect on death, MI or stroke.

frontHtml: 12 independent tests at alpha 0.05 with no true effects: chance of at least one false positive?
No severe liver injury among 300 treated patients: upper 95% limit of the true rate?
What three ingredients make research consent valid?
backHtml: Adequate disclosure, real comprehension and voluntariness.

frontHtml: Must a research consent form promise compensation for research injury?
backHtml: No. For more than minimal risk it must say whether treatment or compensation is available.

frontHtml: Coercion vs undue influence in research recruitment?
backHtml: Coercion: a threat of harm or loss for refusing. Undue influence: an excessive offer that distorts judgment about risk.

frontHtml: What is therapeutic misconception?
backHtml: A participant's belief that research decisions (randomization, fixed doses, placebo) are made for their personal benefit.

frontHtml: Pediatric research: what is needed besides parental permission?
backHtml: The child's assent, an active agreement; failure to object is not assent.

frontHtml: Who consents for an adult who lacks capacity to decide about research?
backHtml: A legally authorized representative as defined by applicable law, with the person's dissent respected.

frontHtml: What must happen before an emergency research study uses the exception from informed consent?
backHtml: IRB approval, community consultation and public disclosure, with independent data monitoring.

frontHtml: Which three types of organizations are HIPAA covered entities?
backHtml: Health plans, health care clearinghouses and providers who conduct standard electronic transactions.

frontHtml: Does the minimum necessary standard apply to disclosures for treatment?
backHtml: No; it applies to payment and operations, not to provider-to-provider treatment disclosures.

frontHtml: Safe harbor de-identification: which date element may remain?
backHtml: Only the year.

frontHtml: What is a limited data set and what does sharing it require?
backHtml: PHI without direct identifiers but with dates, ZIP codes or ages; shared under a data use agreement.

frontHtml: Which notes need specific patient authorization even for payment?
backHtml: Separately kept psychotherapy notes.

frontHtml: Breach of unsecured PHI: deadline to notify affected individuals?
backHtml: Without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery.

frontHtml: Can a practice withhold a patient's records because of an unpaid bill?
backHtml: No; access cannot be conditioned on payment for services.

frontHtml: Minimum IRB membership requirements?
backHtml: At least 5 members, including a scientist, a nonscientist and a member not affiliated with the institution.

frontHtml: Can expedited reviewers disapprove a study?
backHtml: No; only the convened full board can disapprove.

frontHtml: Definition of minimal risk?
backHtml: Harm no greater in probability and magnitude than in daily life or routine physical or psychological examinations.

frontHtml: Under the revised Common Rule, do expedited studies need annual continuing review?
backHtml: Generally no, unless the IRB documents a reason; FDA-regulated studies still do.

frontHtml: Which subparts of 45 CFR 46 protect pregnant women, prisoners and children?
backHtml: B (pregnant women, fetuses, neonates), C (prisoners), D (children).

frontHtml: Federally funded multisite study at US institutions: how many IRBs of record?
backHtml: One: a single IRB.

frontHtml: What extra member must an IRB have when reviewing research involving prisoners?
backHtml: A prisoner or a prisoner representative.

frontHtml: Who sees unblinded interim comparative results in a trial?
backHtml: Only the independent data and safety monitoring board (and its independent statistician).

frontHtml: Why are interim efficacy boundaries stricter than P < 0.05?
backHtml: Repeated looks at accumulating data inflate the overall type I error.

frontHtml: Equal alpha split across 5 planned analyses with overall alpha 0.05?
backHtml: 0.05 ÷ 5 = 0.01 per analysis.

frontHtml: Three reasons a monitoring board may recommend stopping a trial early?
backHtml: Efficacy (overwhelming benefit), harm, or futility.

frontHtml: What bias affects trials stopped early for benefit?
backHtml: They overestimate the size of the treatment effect.

frontHtml: What does a stop for futility show?
backHtml: A meaningful benefit is unlikely; it does not prove equivalence.

frontHtml: What must a sponsor file before first giving a new drug to people in the US?
backHtml: An Investigational New Drug (IND) application; trials may start 30 days later unless the FDA places a clinical hold.

frontHtml: Main purpose and participants of phase I?
backHtml: Safety, tolerability, dose and pharmacokinetics in tens of healthy volunteers (or patients for toxic drugs).

frontHtml: Phase II vs phase III?
backHtml: II: efficacy signal and dose finding in up to a few hundred patients. III: large randomized trials that confirm efficacy.

frontHtml: NDA vs BLA?
backHtml: NDA: small-molecule drugs. BLA: biologics such as antibodies and vaccines.

frontHtml: What obligation comes with accelerated approval?
backHtml: Confirmatory trials to verify clinical benefit predicted by the surrogate end point.

frontHtml: What must a generic drug show for approval?
backHtml: Same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route, and bioequivalence to the reference drug.

frontHtml: What is a REMS?
backHtml: An FDA-required program (medication guide, communication plan, elements to assure safe use) for drugs with serious risks.

frontHtml: Do dietary supplements need FDA approval of safety and efficacy before sale?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: Three forms of research misconduct under US federal policy?
backHtml: Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism.

frontHtml: Fabrication vs falsification?
backHtml: Fabrication invents data; falsification manipulates or omits real data or processes.

frontHtml: Four authorship criteria?
backHtml: Substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, final approval and accountability; all four are required.

frontHtml: What is clinical equipoise?
backHtml: Genuine uncertainty in the expert community about which compared treatment is better.

frontHtml: When is a placebo control acceptable if a proven treatment exists?
backHtml: Only with compelling methodological reasons and no risk of serious or irreversible harm to placebo recipients.

frontHtml: The three Belmont Report principles?
backHtml: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

frontHtml: What does a Certificate of Confidentiality protect against?
backHtml: Compelled disclosure of identifiable sensitive research data, such as by subpoena.

frontHtml: What does teach-back check during research consent?
backHtml: Comprehension: the person explains the study in their own words.

frontHtml: Capacity regained during a study after LAR consent: what next?
backHtml: Ask the participant for their own consent to continue.

frontHtml: A pediatric participant turns 18 during a long study: what is needed?
backHtml: Their own adult consent to continue.

frontHtml: Is stopping the study drug the same as withdrawing from the study?
backHtml: No; ask whether the person also wants to stop visits, follow-up or all contact.

frontHtml: The treating physician is also the investigator: how to reduce pressure to join?
backHtml: State that care will not change if they decline, and let a coordinator or colleague lead consent.

frontHtml: Patient asks for results by unencrypted personal email: allowed?
backHtml: Yes, at the patient's request after a warning about the risks.

frontHtml: Patient paid out of pocket and asks that the visit not go to the insurer: must the provider agree?
backHtml: Yes, for care paid in full out of pocket.

frontHtml: Is browsing a chart without a work reason a violation if nothing is shared?
backHtml: Yes; access needs a legitimate purpose, and audit logs show it.

frontHtml: May the hospital confirm to a caller that a patient is admitted?
backHtml: Only through the facility directory, and only if the patient has not opted out.

frontHtml: How is an inaccurate entry in the record corrected?
backHtml: With a dated addendum; the original entry is never altered or deleted.

frontHtml: Who decides whether a project is research or quality improvement?
backHtml: The institution (usually the IRB office), not the person doing the project.

frontHtml: Participant was consented with an outdated form: fix?
backHtml: Re-consent with the current approved version and report per policy.

frontHtml: Expected adverse event already listed in the consent form: how is it reported?
backHtml: Recorded and reported through routine channels, not as an unanticipated problem.

frontHtml: IRB member who is an investigator on the study under review?
backHtml: Gives information if asked but does not take part in the review or vote.

frontHtml: Is a lost unencrypted research laptop an unanticipated problem?
backHtml: Yes, even though no one was physically harmed.

frontHtml: Four questions to ask of a trial stopped early?
backHtml: Why it stopped, how many events, how big the effect, and what remains unknown.

frontHtml: Trial stopped for harm: what happens to participants in the harmful arm?
backHtml: They are told and stop the intervention under supervision.

frontHtml: What should the report of an early-stopped trial state?
backHtml: The stopping rule, the number of looks and the information fraction at stopping.

frontHtml: What is conditional power?
backHtml: The probability of a significant final result given current data and an assumed future effect.

frontHtml: Is off-label use of an approved drug for one patient research?
backHtml: No; it is clinical care. A systematic study of the use is research.

frontHtml: Where are vaccine adverse events reported?
backHtml: VAERS, run jointly by CDC and FDA.

frontHtml: Can a pharmacist substitute a biosimilar without the prescriber?
backHtml: Only one designated interchangeable, subject to state pharmacy law.

frontHtml: Are compounded drugs FDA-approved products?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: How do current drug labels describe risk in pregnancy?
backHtml: In narrative summaries; the old letter categories are gone.

frontHtml: Who protects a good-faith complainant of research misconduct?
backHtml: The institution's research integrity process, which prohibits retaliation.

frontHtml: A sponsor-paid medical writer drafted the paper: requirement?
backHtml: Disclose the writing support; listed authors must still meet all criteria.

frontHtml: Is disclosure enough to manage every conflict of interest?
backHtml: No; severe conflicts may require limiting the person's role or divestment.

frontHtml: A research laboratory result may guide treatment: what first?
backHtml: Confirm it in a clinically certified laboratory.

frontHtml: Leaving an institution: may you take identifiable research data?
backHtml: Only if the IRB and the data agreements allow it.

frontHtml: Participant expects the investigator to choose the better drug for him: response?
backHtml: Explain that assignment is random and blinded, then recheck understanding.

frontHtml: Research consent with limited English proficiency: who interprets?
backHtml: A qualified medical interpreter with an IRB-approved translated or short-form process, not family.

frontHtml: Child refuses research with no direct benefit; parents want to enrol. Decision?
backHtml: Respect the child's refusal.

frontHtml: Emergency enrolment without consent: family arrives. What next?
backHtml: Tell them about the study promptly; they may end participation.

frontHtml: Capable patient refused disclosure to a relative who calls: response?
backHtml: Share nothing and offer to pass on a message.

frontHtml: Case presentation with dates, town and a facial photo: fix?
backHtml: Use relative days, omit the town and get written authorization for the photo.

frontHtml: Counting eligible patients before writing a protocol: HIPAA pathway?
backHtml: Review preparatory to research, with no PHI removed.

frontHtml: Unencrypted research laptop stolen: first step?
backHtml: Report promptly to the privacy officer and the IRB.

frontHtml: Sponsor wants a new questionnaire added next week: next step?
backHtml: Submit an amendment and wait for IRB approval before use.

frontHtml: Unexpected, possibly related serious event in a trial: reporting?
backHtml: Promptly to the IRB and sponsor.

frontHtml: Participant jailed during a study not approved for prisoners: next step?
backHtml: Pause research contact and notify the IRB.

frontHtml: Research that may benefit only the fetus; father present and capable: whose consent?
backHtml: Both the pregnant woman and the father.

frontHtml: Interim P = 0.02 against a boundary of P < 0.001: conclusion?
backHtml: Boundary not crossed; efficacy not established; continue.

frontHtml: Blinded anticoagulant trial participant bleeding, reversal depends on drug: action?
backHtml: Unblind that participant through the emergency procedure.

frontHtml: Trial stopped early for benefit: best conclusion?
backHtml: Benefit probably real, but the true effect is likely smaller than reported.

frontHtml: Unlisted serious reaction to a new drug: next step?
backHtml: Report to the FDA via MedWatch without waiting for proof.

frontHtml: Uncertified prescriber asked to refill a REMS teratogen without this month's test: response?
backHtml: Arrange the test and a prescription from a certified prescriber.

frontHtml: Patient wants an unapproved drug and no trial is open: route?
backHtml: Request expanded access from the manufacturer and the FDA.

frontHtml: Co-resident invented follow-up data: next step?
backHtml: Report to the PI or research integrity office and preserve the records.

frontHtml: Recent suicide attempter stable on treatment and a placebo washout trial: refer?
backHtml: No; discuss safer options such as add-on or active-control studies.

frontHtml: Three interviewing habits that reduce what patients disclose?
backHtml: Leading questions, several questions at once, and interrupting early.

frontHtml: What two jobs does a summary do in an interview?
backHtml: Checks that you heard correctly and marks a transition to the next part.

frontHtml: Last step of a bad-news conversation?
backHtml: A roadmap: summarise, agree next steps and set the next meeting.

frontHtml: Risk falls from 20% to 15% over 5 years: ARR, RRR and NNT?
Motivational interviewing: what does resistance signal?
backHtml: Change tack; arguing harder produces more push-back.

frontHtml: Who should voice the reasons for change in motivational interviewing?
backHtml: The patient.

frontHtml: Is a smartphone translation app acceptable for a clinical conversation?
backHtml: No; its accuracy for medical content is unverified.

frontHtml: When is video remote interpreting acceptable for a Deaf patient?
backHtml: Only when the picture is clear, real-time and smooth and the patient can follow it.

frontHtml: What should you do before a difficult interpreted conversation (e.g. bad news)?
backHtml: Brief the interpreter beforehand.

frontHtml: Common type of error made by ad hoc (family or untrained) interpreters?
backHtml: Omission, often with clinical consequences.

frontHtml: What does Section 1557 of the ACA add on interpreters?
backHtml: It restricts relying on minors or accompanying adults to interpret, except in emergencies or when the patient asks for an adult companion and that is appropriate.

frontHtml: Which disclosure standard do most US jurisdictions use?
backHtml: What a reasonable patient would want to know.

frontHtml: Treating a capacitated patient without consent vs with inadequate disclosure?
backHtml: Without consent: battery. Inadequate disclosure: negligence.

frontHtml: What is a child's assent?
backHtml: The child's agreement, sought as development allows, alongside the parent's legal consent.

frontHtml: Minor consent for contraception and prenatal care: uniform across states?
backHtml: No; many states allow it, but details vary.

frontHtml: Is a signed consent form the consent?
backHtml: No; it documents the discussion, which is the consent.

frontHtml: What does the Patient Self-Determination Act require?
backHtml: Hospitals must tell patients about their right to make advance directives.

frontHtml: Living will vs durable power of attorney for health care?
backHtml: Living will: instructions for set circumstances. DPOA-HC: names an agent to decide.

frontHtml: Does an unwise or unusual choice prove incapacity?
backHtml: No; it prompts careful assessment, but capacity rests on the four abilities.

frontHtml: Capacity is specific to what two things?
backHtml: The decision and the time (it can fluctuate).

frontHtml: Does leaving against medical advice usually void insurance payment?
backHtml: No; that claim is generally untrue and should not be used as a threat.

frontHtml: Police power vs parens patriae in commitment?
backHtml: Police power: protects others. Parens patriae: protects people who cannot protect themselves.

frontHtml: Can a state confine a nondangerous person who can live safely in freedom?
backHtml: No (US Supreme Court).

frontHtml: May restraint be ordered as needed (PRN)?
backHtml: No; each episode needs its own time-limited order.

frontHtml: Maximum duration of one restraint order for an adult with violent behaviour?
backHtml: Up to 4 hours, renewed only if still needed.

frontHtml: Order of the least restrictive ladder for agitation?
backHtml: De-escalation, then oral medication, then IM medication, then brief restraint or seclusion.

frontHtml: Step 2 CK communication items: what do you respond to first?
backHtml: Strong emotion in the stem.

frontHtml: Patient asks "How long do I have?" First move?
backHtml: Ask what prompts the question, then give an honest range.

frontHtml: Visual aid that helps patients grasp absolute risk?
backHtml: A pictograph of 100 figures.

frontHtml: Motivational interviewing: what do you ask before giving advice?
backHtml: Permission.

frontHtml: How should a family meeting begin?
backHtml: By asking what the family understands so far.

frontHtml: What should you document after an interpreted encounter?
backHtml: The interpreter's name or ID number and the mode used (in person, telephone, video).

frontHtml: Suspected abuse in a patient who needs an interpreter: who interprets?
backHtml: A qualified interpreter, never the partner or a relative who may be involved.

frontHtml: Does a translated consent form replace an interpreted consent discussion?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: An interpreter offers cultural context. What then?
backHtml: Check it with the patient rather than assuming it applies.

frontHtml: When must surgical consent be obtained relative to premedication?
backHtml: Before sedation or premedication impairs the patient.

frontHtml: Does the emergency exception override a valid known refusal of that treatment?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: May a capacitated pregnant woman refuse treatment?
backHtml: Yes; she has the same right to refuse as any capacitated adult.

frontHtml: Adult with intellectual disability: starting presumption about capacity?
backHtml: Presume capacity for the decision at hand and support the person to decide.

frontHtml: Does public reporting of industry payments replace telling the patient about a conflict?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: Vaccine-hesitant parents: usual approach?
backHtml: Explore concerns, inform clearly and keep the relationship; not ordinarily a court matter.

frontHtml: Threshold for a mandated report of child abuse or neglect?
backHtml: Reasonable suspicion, not proof.

frontHtml: Elective, nonurgent surgery for an unemancipated minor needs whose consent?
backHtml: A parent's or guardian's.

frontHtml: How much weight do an adolescent's views carry when parents decide?
backHtml: Increasing weight with maturity; always heard, even when not decisive.

frontHtml: What standard governs decisions for young children?
backHtml: The child's best interests.

frontHtml: What is a POLST-type form?
backHtml: Portable medical orders on resuscitation and life support that travel with a seriously ill patient.

frontHtml: Is a psychiatric hold the tool for a capacitated medical patient refusing treatment?
backHtml: No; holds are for danger caused by mental illness.

frontHtml: Can receiving prescriptions be made conditional on signing an AMA form?
backHtml: No; the form is optional and care is never withheld as punishment.

frontHtml: Patient's wishes, named agent and clinical facts all agree. Need ethics or court?
backHtml: No; act.

frontHtml: What to document for a surrogate decision?
backHtml: Who the surrogate is, why that person has authority, and the evidence of the patient's wishes.

frontHtml: What is monitored while a patient is restrained?
backHtml: Circulation, skin, hydration, toileting and behaviour, continuously.

frontHtml: Can parents sign an adult child into a psychiatric hospital?
backHtml: No; an adult's voluntary status is the adult's own decision.

frontHtml: Is covert medication of a refusing committed patient acceptable?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: Three questions for any hold decision?
backHtml: Mental illness? Danger or grave disability caused by it? A safe less restrictive option?

frontHtml: Before seeking TB detention, which barriers should be addressed?
backHtml: Housing, food, transport and language, plus incentives and directly observed therapy.

frontHtml: Best way to start the history of present illness?
backHtml: An open-ended invitation ("Tell me about…").

frontHtml: Repeats the facts but says they don't apply to him: which ability fails?
backHtml: Appreciation.

frontHtml: Minimum standard of proof for continued civil commitment?
backHtml: Clear and convincing evidence.

frontHtml: Restrained violent patient: how soon a face-to-face evaluation?
backHtml: Within 1 hour.

frontHtml: Federal basis for free language assistance at federally funded providers?
backHtml: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (reinforced by ACA Section 1557).

frontHtml: Minor-consent service available in every state?
backHtml: STI testing and treatment.

frontHtml: Earlier refusal to stay; returns without capacity. Does the refusal bind?
backHtml: No; refusals are decision-specific, so the surrogate decides now.

frontHtml: Interpreter-type cohort study: main threat to a causal conclusion?
backHtml: Confounding by when and where ad hoc interpreters were used.

frontHtml: Why randomize practices, not patients, in a teach-back trial?
backHtml: To prevent contamination of control patients by trained clinicians.

frontHtml: Anxious patient might refuse if told a risk: can it be withheld?
backHtml: No; disclose supportively; therapeutic privilege does not apply.

frontHtml: Living will for terminal illness or permanent unconsciousness; reversible crisis now?
backHtml: The directive does not apply; treat with the agent's agreement.

frontHtml: Restrained patient is calm before the order expires?
backHtml: Remove the restraints now.

frontHtml: Infectious TB, refuses isolation despite DOT and incentives?
backHtml: Health department seeks a legal order for isolation and treatment.

frontHtml: Informed patient prefers her adult daughter to interpret a routine visit?
backHtml: Respect and document it; reconsider for complex topics.

frontHtml: What level of certainty triggers a physician's duty to report suspected child abuse?
backHtml: Reasonable suspicion; proof is not required.

frontHtml: Is a physician liable if a good-faith child abuse report turns out to be unfounded?
backHtml: No. Good-faith reporters are immune from civil and criminal liability.

frontHtml: What is the most common type of substantiated child maltreatment in the US?
backHtml: Neglect.

frontHtml: Which two fracture types in infants are most specific for abuse?
backHtml: Posterior rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions.

frontHtml: Which vessels tear to cause subdural hemorrhage in abusive head trauma?
backHtml: Bridging veins crossing the subdural space.

frontHtml: What does gonorrhea in a prepubertal child (beyond the newborn period) indicate?
backHtml: Sexual contact, i.e. sexual abuse; report to CPS.

frontHtml: To which agency is suspected elder abuse or neglect reported?
backHtml: Adult protective services.

frontHtml: Which ethical principle guides management of IPV disclosed by a competent adult?
backHtml: Respect for autonomy: support and safety-plan; report only where a specific law requires it.

frontHtml: What gestational age range defines periviable birth?
Federally funded sterilization: minimum age and waiting period?
backHtml: Age ≥ 21; consent signed ≥ 30 days (and ≤ 180 days) before surgery.

frontHtml: Is a spouse's consent required for sterilization?
backHtml: No, never.

frontHtml: What do safe-haven laws allow?
backHtml: Anonymous relinquishment of an unharmed newborn at a designated site without prosecution for abandonment.

frontHtml: May parents decline newborn screening?
backHtml: In most states yes (often for religious reasons), after counselling; document the informed refusal.

frontHtml: Can a capacitated pregnant woman refuse a cesarean recommended for the fetus?
backHtml: Yes. Her informed refusal is respected; court orders are not the standard response.

frontHtml: What must a physician with a conscientious objection do?
backHtml: Tell the patient, give accurate information, refer promptly and provide emergency care.

frontHtml: Hospice eligibility: what prognosis must be certified?
backHtml: 6 months or less if the illness runs its usual course (two physicians certify).

frontHtml: Palliative care vs hospice: which allows curative treatment to continue?
backHtml: Palliative care (any stage of serious illness).

frontHtml: Are withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment ethically different?
backHtml: No. They are ethically and legally equivalent.

frontHtml: Which principle justifies opioids for dyspnea that might hasten death?
backHtml: The principle of double effect.

frontHtml: Euthanasia vs medical aid in dying: which is illegal in every US state?
backHtml: Euthanasia (the physician administers the lethal drug).

frontHtml: Name a confounder that must be corrected before determining brain death.
backHtml: Hypothermia (also sedatives, paralytics, severe metabolic disturbance, hypotension).

frontHtml: Do spinal reflexes exclude brain death?
backHtml: No. Spinal reflexes such as triple flexion may persist.

frontHtml: Prolonged grief disorder: minimum time after the death in adults?
backHtml: 12 months (6 months in children and adolescents).

frontHtml: Name the four principles of medical ethics.
backHtml: Respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice.

frontHtml: Does HIPAA require authorization to send records to another treating clinician?
backHtml: No. Treatment, payment and operations need no authorization.

frontHtml: Does the minimum necessary standard apply to disclosures for treatment?
backHtml: No.

frontHtml: Which records need a specific patient authorization even for payment purposes?
backHtml: Psychotherapy notes kept separately from the medical record.

frontHtml: Can a psychiatrist date a former patient after enough time has passed?
backHtml: No. It is unethical regardless of time elapsed.

frontHtml: When is therapeutic privilege justified?
backHtml: Rarely: only when disclosure itself would cause serious, immediate harm; anxiety is not enough.

frontHtml: How long does HIPAA protect a deceased person's health information?
backHtml: 50 years after death.

frontHtml: What is the ACGME weekly work-hour limit?
backHtml: 80 hours per week, averaged over 4 weeks.

frontHtml: Name the three dimensions of burnout.
backHtml: Emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, reduced personal accomplishment.

frontHtml: Is a physician with a well-treated psychiatric illness impaired?
backHtml: No. Impairment is inability to practise safely, not a diagnosis.

frontHtml: What is the first action when a colleague is impaired at work?
backHtml: Stop him or her from caring for patients now and arrange coverage.

frontHtml: What does a state physician health program do?
backHtml: Confidential evaluation, referral to treatment and monitoring; not discipline.

frontHtml: When does a report go to the state licensing board?
backHtml: No institutional route, the colleague refuses help and keeps practising, or patients are harmed.

frontHtml: Which imaging study is required for suspected physical abuse in a child under 2?
backHtml: Skeletal survey (repeat about 2 weeks later).

frontHtml: What is a sentinel injury?
backHtml: A minor injury (e.g. a bruise) in a non-mobile infant that often precedes severe abuse.

frontHtml: Where should IPV screening take place?
backHtml: Privately, with no partner or family present and a professional interpreter if needed.

frontHtml: Name three markers of high lethality risk in IPV.
backHtml: Strangulation, firearms or weapons, threats to kill (also escalation, stalking, recent separation).

frontHtml: How should a patient's account of assault be documented?
backHtml: In her own words in quotation marks, with measured injuries, a body diagram and photographs.

frontHtml: A minor exchanges sex for shelter. How is this classified?
backHtml: Sex trafficking of a minor, reportable as child abuse.

frontHtml: First step when a capacitated pregnant patient refuses a recommended intervention?
backHtml: Explore her reasons and address them; then respect and document an informed refusal.

frontHtml: Treatment of choice for opioid use disorder in pregnancy?
backHtml: Opioid agonist therapy: buprenorphine or methadone.

frontHtml: Can parents refuse an emergency transfusion for their newborn on religious grounds?
backHtml: No. Life-saving emergency treatment for a child is given.

frontHtml: A parent relinquishes a newborn under a safe-haven law. May staff require her name?
backHtml: No. Accept the infant and offer, but do not require, a medical-history form.

frontHtml: Patient asks "What would you do?" after an abnormal prenatal screen. Best first move?
backHtml: Explore her values; counsel non-directively.

frontHtml: Best opening question in a family meeting about bad news?
backHtml: "What do you understand about how she is doing?"

frontHtml: What standard should surrogates use when the patient's wishes are known?
backHtml: Substituted judgment: what the patient would choose.

frontHtml: Should neuromuscular blockers be used during ventilator withdrawal?
backHtml: No. Stop them; titrate opioids to signs of distress.

frontHtml: Does tube feeding prolong life in advanced dementia?
backHtml: No; recommend careful hand feeding.

frontHtml: Who approaches the family about organ donation?
backHtml: The organ procurement organization's trained staff, after the hospital refers the case.

frontHtml: Can a patient leave hospice?
backHtml: Yes. The election can be revoked at any time and re-elected later.

frontHtml: Mother asks for her 17-year-old's STI results. Response?
backHtml: Decline without the adolescent's permission; STI care for minors is confidential.

frontHtml: Family asks you not to tell a capacitated patient her diagnosis. First step?
backHtml: Ask the patient how she wants to receive information and who should be involved.

frontHtml: Patient with HIV refuses to tell his partner. Standard route?
backHtml: Report the case, urge disclosure and use health department partner services.

frontHtml: Can you share information with the family of an incapacitated patient?
backHtml: Yes: information relevant to their involvement in care, when in the patient's interest.

frontHtml: A sibling asks you to prescribe oxycodone. Response?
backHtml: Decline; do not prescribe controlled substances to family; refer to their own clinician.

frontHtml: Colleague off duty drinks heavily once; no work impact. Action?
backHtml: Speak privately, express concern and offer help; report only if practice is affected.

frontHtml: A resident self-discloses alcohol misuse. Program director's next step?
backHtml: Refer to the physician health program and support leave or schedule changes.

frontHtml: Signs of cognitive decline in a senior surgeon. Next step?
backHtml: Report to the chief for a fitness-for-duty evaluation.

frontHtml: Too tired to drive after call. Safe options?
backHtml: Nap in the call room or take a taxi or ride service.

frontHtml: What can a cross-sectional survey of burnout and errors show?
backHtml: Association, but not direction or causation.

frontHtml: Medicaid patient: consent signed 18 days before a scheduled term cesarean. Can sterilization be done at the cesarean?
backHtml: No. The 30-day wait is not met, and a scheduled term cesarean is not an exception.

frontHtml: Weekly hours 86, 78, 84, 70: does the resident meet the 80-hour rule?
backHtml: Yes: average 79.5 hours over 4 weeks.

frontHtml: Burnout 96/480 vs no burnout 72/720 with errors: prevalence ratio?
backHtml: 20% ÷ 10% = 2.0 (the odds ratio would be 2.25).

frontHtml: Parents ask to keep ventilating their son after brain death is declared. What do you say first?
backHtml: Tell them clearly and kindly that he has died.

frontHtml: Symmetric circumferential burns of both feet with sharp tide lines suggest what?
backHtml: Forced immersion (inflicted burn).

frontHtml: Which request needs no authorization: employer, son, health department, life insurer, neighbour?
backHtml: The health department, for a reported disease.

frontHtml: What four elements must a plaintiff prove in a medical negligence claim?
backHtml: Duty, breach of the standard of care, causation and damages.

frontHtml: How is the standard of care defined?
backHtml: What a reasonably prudent physician in the same specialty would do in similar circumstances.

frontHtml: What standard of proof applies in a civil malpractice case?
backHtml: Preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not).

frontHtml: Which doctrine allows negligence to be inferred from a retained surgical sponge?
backHtml: Res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself").

frontHtml: Which doctrine makes a hospital liable for its employed nurse's negligence?
backHtml: Respondeat superior (vicarious liability).

frontHtml: What do Good Samaritan laws protect, and what do they not protect?
